# TypeScript - Prerequisites check

Today names a pattern you have already half-built. The TypeScript underneath it is all
class syntax.

| Concept | Taught in |
|---|---|
| `class`, `constructor`, `this` | [week3/day3_1](/learn/w3/d3/p1) |
| `readonly` and `private` fields | [week3/day3_1](/learn/w3/d3/p1) |
| `extends` and `super()` | new - below |
| `abstract` classes | new - below |
| `protected` | new - below |

**Next:** [Fundamentals - The Page Object Model](/learn/w5/d3/p2)

## Concept 1 - `extends` and `super()`

A subclass inherits every field and method of its parent. `super(...)` calls the parent's
constructor, and TypeScript makes you call it **before** touching `this`.

| Rule | Why |
|---|---|
| `super()` comes first | the parent sets up the fields you are about to use |
| Skipping it | compile error, not a silent bug |

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Concept 2 - three visibility keywords

| Keyword | Reachable from |
|---|---|
| `public` (the default) | anywhere |
| `protected` | this class **and its subclasses** |
| `private` | this class only |

`protected` is the one that matters today: a base page holds the `page` object, subclasses need
it, and tests should not reach past the class to grab it.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Concept 3 - `abstract`

An `abstract` class exists only to be extended. `new BasePage(page)` is a compile error - which
is exactly what you want for a class that is plumbing rather than a page.

```ts
export abstract class BasePage {
  protected readonly page: Page;
  constructor(page: Page) { this.page = page; }
}
```

> **Which tool actually stops you.** Nothing at run time does - `abstract` vanishes when the types
> are stripped, so this lesson's kernel, and even `deno run`, will construct one happily. The
> **type-checker** is what refuses:
>
> ```
> error TS2511: Cannot create an instance of an abstract class.
> ```
>
> from `npx tsc --noEmit` or `deno check`. That is the tool CI runs, which is what makes the
> guarantee real - but it is also why you will never see this fail in a lesson cell.

**Next:** [Fundamentals - The Page Object Model](/learn/w5/d3/p2)

# Fundamentals - The Page Object Model

You built a `LoginPage` class in [week3/day3_2](/learn/w3/d3/p2) because three tests kept
repeating the same lines. Today that gets its name - the **Page Object Model** - and, more
usefully, its **rules**.

> **Follow this one in your own project.** These examples are run by the Playwright test runner, which the editor here does not provide. Copy them into your own checkout to run them.

## Step 1 - measure the problem first

Here is a spec with no page objects. It passes. Nothing about it is wrong.

Now count, in that one file:

| Detail | Times written |
|---|---|
| `"Enter Email"` | 3 |
| `"Enter Password"` | 3 |
| `"Login"` button | 3 |
| `"**/dashboard"` | 3 |

**Twelve edits** when the login form is redesigned - in a file with three tests. A real suite has
three hundred. That is the cost the pattern removes, and it is worth stating as a number rather
than as "it's cleaner".

## Step 2 - the three rules

| # | Rule | Consequence if you break it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | One class per page (or per meaningful region) | a 900-line God class nobody can find anything in |
| 2 | Locators are fields; actions are methods named for what a *person* does | tests read like DOM scripts again |
| 3 | **No `expect()` inside the class** | the class can only ever test the happy path |

Rule 3 is the one people break first and the one that pays. Watch what it buys in Step 5.

## Step 3 - the base class

Plumbing every page needs, and nothing else.

`abstract`, `protected page`, and two members: `goto()` and `section()`. Resist adding more. The
moment `BasePage` knows what a payee is, it has stopped being a base class.
## Step 4 - two page classes

Two details worth stopping on:

- **`DashboardPage.tiles` is `p.card-text`.** The dashboard tiles are paragraphs, not links -
  `getByRole("link")` finds nothing on this page. A real quirk, absorbed by the class so that no
  test has to know it. This is the pattern earning its keep.
- **`LoginPage` has two sign-in methods.** `signIn()` waits for a dashboard; `signInExpectingRefusal()`
  does not, because a refused login never reaches one.
## Step 5 - the same three journeys, and why rule 3 matters

Steps 1-3 of that spec are the inline spec rewritten. **Step 4 is the payoff:** it reuses
`LoginPage` to check that a *bad* password is refused.

That only works because `signIn()` asserts nothing. Had the class ended with
`await expect(page).toHaveURL(/dashboard/)`, it could never test a failed login - you would write
a second class, or give up and go inline. One assertion inside a page object costs you half its
uses.

Step 5 shows the inherited half: neither page class defines `goto()` or `section()`, and both
have them.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## What POM does *not* solve

| Limitation | What it means |
|---|---|
| A redesign that moves a control to another page | the method moves too; tests that called it break |
| Non-programmers still cannot write tests | it is TypeScript either way - see [day5_2](/learn/w5/d5/p2) |
| Over-abstraction | `dashboardPage.doTheThing()` hiding 40 lines is not readable, just short |

The honest summary: POM makes markup changes cheap. It does not make *behaviour* changes cheap,
and nothing does.

**Next:** [Implementation - How a real repo shapes it](/learn/w5/d3/p3)

# Implementation - How a real repo shapes it

Same classes, same locators-as-fields - arranged so that a suite of 300 tests stays navigable.

## Folder shape

```
tests/
  pages/
    BasePage.ts
    LoginPage.ts
    DashboardPage.ts
    components/
      Header.ts            <- appears on every page; not a page itself
      TransactionTable.ts
  fixtures/
    test.ts                <- the one import every spec uses  (day4_2)
  specs/
    login.spec.ts
```

`section()` was never written in `Dashboard` and `signOut()` never will be. One came down the
inheritance chain, the other is reached through a field - and the call sites read differently on
purpose: `dash.section()` versus `dash.header.signOut()`.

## Inheritance or composition?

| Use | When |
|---|---|
| `extends BasePage` | *is-a*: LoginPage **is a** page |
| `new Header(page)` field | *has-a*: DashboardPage **has a** header |

Deep inheritance chains (`AdminDashboardPage extends DashboardPage extends BasePage`) are where
POM suites go to die - a change three levels up breaks pages you have not read. Keep the chain
one level deep and compose the rest.

## Reviewer's checklist

| Look for | Because |
|---|---|
| `expect(` in a `pages/` file | rule 3 - it halves the class's uses |
| A locator string in a spec file | the abstraction has a hole |
| `page.waitForTimeout` anywhere | a hidden race, not a fix |
| A method named `clickSubmitButton` | named for the DOM, not for the user |
| A class over ~150 lines | probably two pages, or a page plus a component |

**Next:** [Practice](/learn/w5/d3/p4)

# Practice - Practice

Work in `week5/generated/`. Add to `pages/` rather than editing the classes you were given, so
the [Fundamentals](/learn/w5/d3/p2) cells still run.
**Next:** [Day 4 - TypeScript - Prerequisites](/learn/w5/d4/p1)

problems.statement:
**Count it yourself**
Before writing any code: count how many separate edits `day3-inline.spec.ts` needs if the email
field's placeholder becomes `"Email address"`. Then count the same for `day3-pom.spec.ts`.

**Right when:** you have two numbers and can point at every line in each.

**A PayBillsPage**
The Pay Bills tile leads to `/paymentDashboard`. Write `pages/PayBillsPage.ts` extending
`BasePage`, with at least two locators and one action.

**Right when:** a new spec reaches that page through `DashboardPage.openTile` and asserts one of
your locators is visible - with no CSS or placeholder text in the spec file.

**Break rule 3 on purpose**
Add `await expect(this.page).toHaveURL(/dashboard/)` to the end of `signIn()` in a *copy* of
`LoginPage`. Then try to write the bad-password test with it.

**Right when:** you can state exactly what goes wrong, and which of the two methods you now need
to add back.

**A Header component**
Extract the logout button into `pages/components/Header.ts` and compose it into `DashboardPage`.

**Right when:** a spec calls `dashboardPage.header.signOut()` and passes, and `DashboardPage` no
longer mentions the logout button's selector.

**Try to construct the abstract class**
Write `const b = new BasePage(page);` in a spec and run `npx tsc --noEmit`. Then run the same line
through `deno run`.

**Right when:** the first gives you `TS2511` and the second prints happily - and you can explain
the difference in one sentence.

**protected versus private**
Change `protected readonly page` in `BasePage` to `private`, then run `npx tsc --noEmit`.

**Right when:** you can name every file that breaks and say why `protected` was the right choice.
Change it back.

**The returning-page style**
Rewrite `signIn()` in a copy of `LoginPage` so it returns a `DashboardPage`. Write one spec in
that style.

**Right when:** it passes, *and* you can describe the import cycle you would create if
`DashboardPage` also returned a `LoginPage` from `signOut()`.
